1016.title: Hamsa, the mantra in every breath
1016.hook: a yoga Upanishad hears hamsa in every breath, and teachers turn it into so'ham: I am That
1016.carry: so'ham: every breath says i am that
1016.tomorrow: why would silent japa count most?
1016.howItsDone: Some Hindu yoga teachers teach ajapa japa, listening to the breath's own sound as hamsa or so'ham, often read as 'I am That', and letting a chosen mantra move with the in-breath and out-breath.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana at sandhya: prayer at the joints of the day: standing until the sun shows, sitting until the stars appear.
screen: `MANTRA SADHANA.` · `SANDHYA: PRAYER AT THE JOINTS OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Ha, on the way out. Sa, on the way in. Breathe out slowly through the nose, and the air makes a soft sound, close to an h. Breathe in, and there's a faint hiss, close to an s. Easy to miss; it's just breath. But some yoga texts heard something more. To them, that soft sound was a mantra, repeated day and night by every breathing creature, without anyone choosing to say it.
screen: `HA, ON THE WAY OUT.` → `SA, ON THE WAY IN.` → `A MANTRA NOBODY SAYS.`

segments.voice: The text is the Dhyanabindu Upanishad, one of the yoga Upanishads. In paraphrase: the breath goes out with the sound ha and comes back in with the sound sa, and so the living being is always repeating hamsa, hamsa. This, it says, is called the ajapa gayatri. Ajapa means not-japa: repetition that happens without effort, with no beads, no lips, no count. Hamsa is also the Sanskrit word for a swan or a wild goose, and in Indian poetry the swan can sip the milk out of milk mixed with water. So it became a picture of a soul that can tell the real from the passing, and the greatest renunciates are given the title paramahamsa, the supreme swan. Some teachers turn the sound around: so'ham, I am That. Vedanta teachers hear in those two syllables one of this path's biggest ideas: the Self in you, the atman, is not finally separate from Brahman, the one reality in everything. Read that way, every breathing creature says it all day, a sparrow, a grandmother, a baby asleep, and almost nobody hears. For four days this practice has been about keeping a mantra going: setting terms, counting beads, tying it to dawn and dusk. Ajapa adds something quieter. The repetition isn't only the one you push. It's also the one you finally hear. Some teachers keep the beads and the chosen mantra and let it ride on the breath, one part on the out-breath, one on the in. The discipline stays. It just rides on a sound that was already saying who you are.
screen: `HA OUT, SA IN: HAMSA.` · `AJAPA: THE JAPA NOT DONE.` · `THE SWAN THAT TELLS MILK FROM WATER.` · `SO'HAM: I AM THAT.` · then, large: `THE ATMAN IS NOT SEPARATE FROM BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Let the breath move through the nose, no counting, and listen: a soft ha on the out-breath, a faint sa on the in, not made any louder. If you've been keeping a mantra, let it rest on that sound, part on the out-breath and part on the in; if not, stay with hamsa, or with the breath's own sound. When the mind drifts, come back to listening.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, ajapa: the mantra the breath keeps by itself, hamsa, so'ham, I am That.
screen: `MANTRA SADHANA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: so'ham, every breath says I am That. The atman and Brahman, in two syllables. I'll be here tomorrow.

1017.title: Aloud, whispered, silent
1017.hook: Krishna calls japa his own offering, and an old law book ranks the silent kind highest
1017.carry: japa is an offering, even in silence
1017.tomorrow: can a name said wrong still work?
1017.howItsDone: Hindus who keep japa may say the mantra aloud, in a whisper or silently in the mind, often counting on a mala of beads; some move between these voices within one sitting.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana and ajapa: the mantra the breath keeps by itself, ha on the way out, sa on the way in.
screen: `MANTRA SADHANA.` · `ONE MANTRA, DAY AFTER DAY.`

segments.voice: Dawn, one house, three people, the same mantra. In the kitchen a grandmother says it out loud while the kettle heats, each syllable clear from the hallway. On the back step her grandson whispers it, the sound barely past his teeth. Upstairs his mother sits on the edge of the bed with her eyes closed, and nothing moves at all. No lips, no breath out of rhythm. Walk through that house and you'd only know two of them were doing japa. All three are. An old law book sets those three voices in an order, and the order runs against the ear.
screen: `ONE HOUSE. ONE MANTRA.` → `ALOUD. WHISPERED. SILENT.` → `ALL THREE ARE JAPA.`

segments.voice: Japa is repetition: a mantra said again and again, often counted on a string of beads. In the Bhagavad Gita, chapter ten, Arjuna asks Krishna a simple question: in what forms should I think of you? Krishna names the best of many things, and among sacrifices, he says, he is the sacrifice of japa: the offering made of a word. That's the teaching under every mala. Japa isn't a drill. It's yajna, an offering, the same word used for offerings poured into the sacred fire, made of nothing but a name. The law book called the Manusmriti then ranks the ways of making it. In its second chapter it says japa is stronger than the prescribed rites. Japa spoken so that others can't hear it is stronger still. And japa done in the mind alone is the strongest of the three. Manu calls the quiet form upamshu, sound kept close to the lips, and the silent one manasa, of the mind. Teachers call the spoken form vachika. So the quietest voice in the house is the one the text sets highest. Some teachers read it this way: when the mantra is loud, the ear holds it for you. Whispered, the lips still help. Silent, the mind has nothing to lean on but the mind. For a long sadhana, some teachers suggest moving between the voices rather than forcing silence: back to a whisper when attention scatters, silent when it settles. Read that way, the grandmother in the kitchen and the mother upstairs are making the same offering.
screen: `IN WHAT FORMS SHOULD I THINK OF YOU?` · `AMONG SACRIFICES, I AM JAPA.` · `SPOKEN, WHISPERED, MENTAL.` · `MOVE BETWEEN THEM AS THE MIND NEEDS.` · then, large: `AN OFFERING MADE OF A WORD.`

segments.voice: Take the mantra you've been keeping, or the syllable Om, or a single word from your own tradition, and say it aloud a few times, gently. Let it become a whisper, lips moving, then close the lips and keep it going inside, with no sound at all. If the mind wanders, go back to the whisper for a while, then let it go silent again.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, the three voices it can be kept in: spoken, whispered and silent.
screen: `MANTRA SADHANA — today's word`.

1018.title: The robber and the name
1018.hook: a robber who can't say the name Rama is told to say it backwards, until an anthill grows over him
1018.carry: the name, kept long and with love
1018.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep nama japa, repeating a name of God such as Rama, Krishna or Shiva, often on a mala; those who take on a mantra sadhana may keep it at the same time each day, and customs differ on what happens if a day is lost.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana in three voices: japa is an offering, even in silence, with the silent one set highest.
screen: `MANTRA SADHANA.` · `JAPA IS AN OFFERING, EVEN IN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: On day seven you met a robber on a forest road who asked his family to share the weight of his deeds, and they wouldn't. Here's a part of his story that day left out. He comes back to the sage shaken: what do I do now? The sage gives him a word to repeat. Rama. And he can't say it. A life of violence, the telling goes, has left the holy name stuck in his throat. So the sage turns it around. Say mara, then. Mara, mara, mara. He sits down and says it, and the backwards word runs together: mara-mara-mara, rama-rama, Rama.
screen: `A ROBBER. A HOLY NAME.` → `HE CAN'T SAY IT.` → `MARA, MARA, MARA.`

segments.voice: He sits so long that an anthill grows over him. When he finally rises, the story says, he is Valmiki, named for valmika, the anthill, and he will sing the Ramayana. This telling is later than the Ramayana itself, and versions differ on the sage. But many Hindus tell it to say something they believe deeply: the name of God works even when it's said badly. What matters is that it's kept. This is nama japa, repeating a name of God, Rama, Krishna, Shiva, and for many Hindus it is the heart of daily practice. Patanjali puts the same thing in two short lines. Practice becomes firmly rooted, sutra one fourteen says in paraphrase, when it is kept up for a long time, without a break, and with care. The word for care is satkara, which carries honor and devotion. A little later he names the word itself: the word that expresses Ishvara, the Lord, is the syllable Om, and its japa goes with dwelling on its meaning. Repeat it, and turn toward what it points to. Notice what neither the story nor the sutra counts. Not perfect pronunciation. Not a number of days; forty is a shape teachers and families give a sadhana. Customs differ on what a lost day means for a vow, so ask the teacher or the elder whose practice it is. What both hold onto is the long arc and the love. A robber who could only say the name backwards became the poet of God.
screen: `AN ANTHILL GROWS OVER HIM.` · `NAMA JAPA: A NAME OF GOD, REPEATED.` · `A LONG TIME. NO BREAK. WITH CARE.` · `OM: REPEAT IT, DWELL ON ITS MEANING.` · then, large: `THE NAME, KEPT LONG, WITH LOVE.`

segments.voice: Take the mantra you've been keeping, or a name of God you love, or the syllable Om, and repeat it slowly. Don't worry about saying it perfectly. Between repetitions, let a moment go to what it points toward: if you pray, that pointing can be your prayer, and if you don't, simply rest in the pause after the sound.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline, which, from Valmiki's anthill to Patanjali's sutra, grows firm through a long time and care.
screen: `MANTRA SADHANA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the name, kept long and with love. Even said backwards, it carried a robber home. Tomorrow, a sleep with its own name. See you then.

1019.title: The Goddess who holds Vishnu's sleep
1019.hook: Vishnu sleeps on the cosmic waters, two demons rise to kill Brahma, and Brahma has to wake him
1019.carry: shakti: even vishnu rests in her power
1019.tomorrow: what is the fourth state, past deep sleep?
1019.howItsDone: Hindus who recite the Devi Mahatmya, especially during Navaratri, read Brahma's hymn to Yoganidra in its first chapter; some temples and households chant the whole text over several days.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed mantra sadhana with Patanjali: practice grows firm through the name, kept long and with love.
screen: `MANTRA SADHANA.` · `A LONG TIME. NO BREAK. WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: Everything is water. One age of the world has ended, and the next hasn't begun. On that ocean, on the coils of a great serpent, Vishnu lies asleep. From his navel rises a lotus, and on the lotus sits Brahma, the one who will make the next world. Then two demons, Madhu and Kaitabha, rise out of the dark and come for Brahma. He looks down at the one person who could help him, and Vishnu doesn't stir. This sleep isn't ordinary. It has a name, and the name is today's word.
screen: `ONE OCEAN. VISHNU ASLEEP.` → `TWO DEMONS COME FOR BRAHMA.` → `THE SLEEP HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: The story opens the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a text set inside the Markandeya Purana. Brahma doesn't shake Vishnu. He doesn't shout. He turns to the power that is holding Vishnu asleep, and he praises her. The text calls her Yoganidra. Yoga nidra: the sleep of yoga. In this story she isn't a technique. She is the Goddess herself, the great power behind creation, its keeping and its ending. This is Shakti, power, and for Hindus who worship the Goddess as supreme, it's the deepest truth there is: the divine is power, and that power is a mother. Brahma's hymn calls her by many names, among them the great night and the night of delusion, and also intelligence and understanding. Then he asks her to let Vishnu go. And she does. The text says she withdraws from his eyes, his mouth, his nose, his arms, his heart and his chest, and the Lord of the world rises to fight Madhu and Kaitabha. That's why the text is the Glory of the Goddess, even though Vishnu does the fighting: without her, the preserver of the world can't open his eyes. And it's why, every Navaratri, temples and homes chant these chapters. So yoga nidra, on this path, begins not as a technique but as a picture: a sleep that isn't absence, held by her.
screen: `BRAHMA PRAISES THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE SLEEP.` · `YOGANIDRA IS THE GODDESS HERSELF.` · `SHAKTI: THE POWER IN EVERYTHING.` · `SHE LEAVES HIS EYES, HIS HEART. HE RISES.` · then, large: `EVEN VISHNU RESTS IN HER POWER.`

segments.voice: Lie down, or lean back in your chair, and let the body be heavy, as if resting on water. Follow the story's waking slowly, in reverse: the chest rising and falling, the heart, the arms resting, the nose with the breath moving in it, the mouth soft, the eyes still behind the lids. Don't try to sleep and don't try to stay alert; just rest and notice.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. In the Devi Mahatmya, it's the Goddess herself, holding Vishnu asleep on the waters.
screen: `YOGA NIDRA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Shakti, even Vishnu rests in her power. A sleep so full it has its own hymn. That's today, done.

1020.title: Waking, dreaming, sleep, and the fourth
1020.hook: Hanuman asks Rama how anyone gets free, and Rama names one short Upanishad about a single night
1020.carry: the self that wakes, dreams and sleeps is brahman
1020.tomorrow: what light do you see by in the dark?
1020.howItsDone: Hindus who study Vedanta read the Mandukya Upanishad's four states and its saying 'this Self is Brahman', sometimes with Gaudapada's Karika beside it; some chant Om slowly, resting in the silence after the sound.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra began on the cosmic waters: Vishnu asleep, held by the Goddess Yoganidra, and Brahma praising her to wake him.
screen: `YOGA NIDRA.` · `THE GODDESS WHO HOLDS THE SLEEP.`

segments.voice: In Ayodhya, after the war, Hanuman sits at Rama's feet and asks what every seeker asks: how does anyone get free? Back in year one you heard Rama's answer: one Upanishad is enough, if you truly take it in. In the Muktika Upanishad he names that one. The Mandukya. And it isn't about heaven, or battles, or gods. It's about something you'll do tonight. Lights out, and the to-do list lets go. Pictures start arriving on their own. Later even the pictures stop. Then morning. Waking, dreaming, deep sleep. And then the Mandukya says there's a fourth.
screen: `HOW DOES ANYONE GET FREE?` → `ONE UPANISHAD IS ENOUGH.` → `WAKING. DREAMING. SLEEP. AND A FOURTH.`

segments.voice: The Mandukya begins with a word from the mantra days just behind us: Om. All this is Om, it says. Then, in its second verse, one of the great sayings of the Upanishads: this Self is Brahman. Ayam atma brahma. The you behind your eyes is not finally other than the reality behind everything. And this Self, it says, has four quarters. In paraphrase: the first is waking, knowing outward, enjoying the world of things. The second is dreaming, knowing inward, enjoying what is subtle. The third is deep sleep, where the sleeper wants nothing and sees no dream. The text doesn't call it empty. It calls it a gathered mass of knowing, full of bliss, the doorway to knowledge. And then the fourth, turiya, described mostly by what it is not. Not knowing outward, not knowing inward, not a mass of knowing. Unseen, beyond grasp, peaceful, one without a second. That, it says, is the Self, and that is what is to be known. Then it maps the four onto Om. The A is waking. The U is dreaming. The M is deep sleep. The fourth has no part at all; some teachers hear it as the silence after Om ends. So every night you pass through three rooms, and the same Self is there in each. Advaita teachers read it this way: freedom isn't a place you travel to. It's knowing what was there all along. And yoga nidra, resting awake on the borders between those rooms, is one way to notice.
screen: `AYAM ATMA BRAHMA: THIS SELF IS BRAHMAN.` · `WAKING, DREAMING, DEEP SLEEP.` · `THE FOURTH: NOT IN, NOT OUT. PEACEFUL.` · `A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE.` · then, large: `ONE SELF IN EVERY ROOM.`

segments.voice: Say Om once, slowly, aloud or in the mind: feel the A open in the throat, the U round in the mouth, the M hum at the closed lips. Then let it end and stay in the quiet after it, letting thoughts come like pictures at the edge of sleep. When it feels right, say Om once more, and rest again in the silence that follows.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, resting on the borders the Mandukya maps: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth beyond them.

1021.title: The light when every light goes out
1021.hook: a king asks a sage what light a person sees by when the sun, moon and fire are all gone
1021.carry: the self is its own light
1021.tomorrow: who asked for sleep instead of a boon?
1021.howItsDone: Hindus who study the Upanishads read Janaka's questions to Yajnavalkya on the light of the Self and on dream and deep sleep; teachers of yoga nidra describe the practice as resting deeply while staying aware.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra and the Mandukya's map: the self that wakes, dreams and sleeps is brahman.
screen: `YOGA NIDRA.` · `WAKING, DREAMING, SLEEP, THE FOURTH.`

segments.voice: A king named Janaka puts a question to the sage Yajnavalkya. What light does a person see by? The sun, says the sage. By its light we sit, go out, work, and come home. And when the sun has set? The moon. And when the moon has set? Fire. And when the fire goes out? Then speech: in the dark, we move toward a voice. And when speech, too, falls silent? The king keeps pushing, the way a child keeps asking why. The answer is where this Upanishad turns toward sleep.
screen: `WHAT LIGHT DOES A PERSON SEE BY?` → `SUN. MOON. FIRE. SPEECH.` → `AND WHEN ALL OF THEM ARE GONE?`

segments.voice: This is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, chapter four, and Yajnavalkya's answer, in paraphrase, is this: then the Self is his light. By that light he sits, goes out, works and comes home. This is one of the Upanishads' great teachings about the atman: the Self isn't lit by anything. It is the light everything else is seen by. Then the sage follows the person into sleep. In dreams, he says, there are no chariots, no harnesses, no roads, but the dreamer makes chariots and harnesses and roads. There are no joys or ponds or rivers, and the dreamer makes those too. In dream, the text says, the person becomes his own light. Nothing outside lights the scene; it's lit from within. Then comes the image this whole yoga nidra stretch could rest on. A falcon, or any swift bird, has been flying around in the open sky. It grows tired. It folds its wings and is carried down to its nest. In the same way, the sage says, a person hurries toward that state where, asleep, there's no more wanting and no more dreaming. Deep sleep, here, isn't collapse. It's a homecoming. So when a teacher of yoga nidra asks a room to stop doing and let the body grow heavy, they're inviting something this Upanishad already pictured. What the practice adds is staying aware as it happens: the falcon lands, and the light that is the Self watches it land.
screen: `THEN THE SELF IS HIS LIGHT.` · `THE ATMAN IS THE LIGHT EVERYTHING IS SEEN BY.` · `IN DREAMS, THE PERSON IS HIS OWN LIGHT.` · `THE TIRED FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS.` · then, large: `THE SELF IS ITS OWN LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Lie down, or let the chair take your weight, and let the day so far be a long flight: all the reaching, answering, carrying. On one out-breath let the shoulders fall, as if folding wings; on the next, let the hands go slack; on the next, the jaw. Each out-breath, a little more landing, and stay aware of it happening.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. Today, the Self that lights even our dreams, and the falcon folding its wings to go home.

1022.title: Kumbhakarna's sleep
1022.hook: a giant opens his mouth to ask the Creator for a boon, and what comes out is: let me sleep
1022.carry: too much sleep is tamas, not yoga
1022.tomorrow: why make a resolve before you rest?
1022.howItsDone: Hindu families retell Kumbhakarna's sleep from the Ramayana, often to tease a late riser; students of the Gita and the Yoga Sutras read Gita 6.16–17 and 14.8 on sleep and tamas, and Yoga Sutra 1.10 on sleep as a movement of the mind.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra and Janaka's question: when every light goes out, the Self is its own light.
screen: `YOGA NIDRA.` · `THE SELF IS ITS OWN LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Three brothers do fierce austerities, and Brahma, the Creator, comes to grant each a boon. One is Ravana. One is Vibhishana. The third is Kumbhakarna, a giant so huge and so hungry that the gods are terrified of what he'll ask for. So, in the Ramayana's telling, Brahma calls on Sarasvati, the goddess of speech, and she slips into the giant's mouth. Kumbhakarna opens it to ask his boon, and what comes out is: let me sleep for many years. And he does.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS. THREE BOONS.` → `THE GODDESS OF SPEECH IN HIS MOUTH.` → `LET ME SLEEP.`

segments.voice: A well-loved retelling makes it a slip of the tongue: he meant to ask for indrasana, Indra's throne, and said nidrasana, a bed of sleep. Brahma softens the boon only a little: six months asleep, one day awake. When Rama's army reaches Lanka, it takes drums, shouting and elephants to wake him. He tells Ravana plainly that he's in the wrong, then fights for his brother anyway, and falls. To this day Hindu families tease a late sleeper by calling him Kumbhakarna. Now set him beside Vishnu, three days ago, asleep on the waters. Two sleepers, two kinds of sleep. Vishnu's is yoga nidra, held by the Goddess, and he rises the moment she lets him go. Kumbhakarna's is heaviness, a sleep that swallows most of a life. The Gita has a name for that heaviness: tamas, the quality of dullness, which, Krishna says, binds a person through carelessness, laziness and sleep. And in chapter six he says yoga isn't for one who sleeps too much, or for one who never sleeps; it's for one moderate in sleep and in waking. Patanjali adds a sober note. In the Yoga Sutras he lists five movements of the mind, the vrittis, and sleep is one: the movement that rests on the experience of absence. Deep sleep isn't stillness. Some commentators point to the morning: we wake and say, I slept well, I knew nothing. Something registered that nothing. So drifting off isn't yoga. Rest with someone awake inside it is: Vishnu's kind, not Kumbhakarna's.
screen: `HE MEANT A THRONE. HE ASKED FOR SLEEP.` · `TWO SLEEPERS: VISHNU AND KUMBHAKARNA.` · `TAMAS BINDS THROUGH SLEEP.` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE.` · then, large: `SLEEP IS STILL A MOVEMENT OF THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Lie down or sit back and let the body grow heavy, and when a wave of drowsiness comes, notice it as a movement, the way you'd notice a thought: heaviness arriving, heaviness passing. If you begin to drift, don't fight it hard; come back to the breath at the nose, then watch the heaviness return. Resting and watching, both at once.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga: rest with awareness inside it. Vishnu's sleep, not Kumbhakarna's.
screen: `YOGA NIDRA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: too much sleep is tamas, not yoga. Vishnu rests and rises; Kumbhakarna just sleeps. See you tomorrow.
